# The Taro Yamane Formula {#sec-yamane}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Learning objectives"}
- State the formula and its conventional approximations.
- Identify circumstances in which it should not be used.
:::

## The idea

The widely circulated **Yamane simplified formula** uses the finite population size $N$ and a selected error quantity $e$: $n=N/(1+Ne^2)$. It is commonly presented in introductory survey contexts as a simplified approximation broadly associated with 95% confidence and maximum variance for a proportion. These conditions are not replaceable by arbitrary confidence and prevalence inputs without returning to a more general method.

## When and how to apply it

Yamane should not be applied automatically to clinical trials, diagnostic sensitivity targets, cohort associations, complex surveys or estimation objectives requiring design-specific corrections. It is not a universal substitute for justifying the underlying estimand, sampling design and precision.

## Formula at a glance

$$
n=\frac{N}{1+Ne^2}
$$


## Teaching case 1 — baseline draft

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Clinical scenario / initial worked example"}
For $N=1000$ and $e=0.05$, the formula yields $1000/(1+1000\times0.05^2)=285.71$, rounded upward to **286** complete observations.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Calculation logic

The example uses the stated planning assumptions and mathematical approximation. Explain why they apply before reporting the numerical result.

### Copy-and-run R

```r
N <- 1000; e <- .05
ceiling(N / (1 + N * e^2))
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Common error"}
This simplified result is not generally numerically identical to an explicitly specified general finite-population-adjusted proportion calculation.
:::
